analysis.one_liner: Bans PFAS "forever chemicals" in food packaging sold in interstate commerce.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 22 cosponsors including one Republican, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to make it illegal to sell food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS — man-made "forever chemicals" often used to make wrappers and containers grease- and water-resistant. These chemicals persist in the environment and accumulate in people's bodies, and they are commonly found in fast-food wrappers, takeout containers, and other food contact materials. The ban would have taken effect January 1, 2025. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat packaged and restaurant food — effectively everyone — would get reduced exposure to PFAS, which accumulate in the body over time and have been linked in scientific studies to health harms including immune, liver, and developmental effects. States, water utilities, and taxpayers would also face less PFAS contamination entering the environment through discarded packaging. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who eats packaged or restaurant food

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the sale of food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS by amending the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act's prohibited-acts list, making it a federal violation to introduce such packaging into interstate commerce.

Defines PFAS broadly as any man-made perfluoroalkyl or polyfluoroalkyl substance with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom, closing off easy loopholes with replacement chemicals that are similar but slightly altered.
Set the ban to begin January 1, 2025, giving manufacturers immediate notice rather than a long phase-in, since several states had already moved to ban PFAS in food packaging.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that produce PFAS and packaging makers that use it for grease resistance would lose a market and bear reformulation costs. Food businesses — including small restaurants and grocers — could face somewhat higher packaging costs as suppliers switch to alternatives. [S2]

drawbacks.text: PFAS coatings give food packaging cheap, effective grease and water resistance, and safer alternatives can cost more — a cost that could pass through to restaurants and grocery prices, hitting small food businesses hardest.

The ban covers the entire class of PFAS regardless of which specific compounds or exposure levels are involved, a blanket approach that some in industry argue sweeps in substances with little demonstrated food-contact risk; however, its scientifically defensible core is that PFAS do not break down and accumulate in people and the environment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit is structural: PFAS never break down, so every package sold adds to a permanent body and environmental burden, and the bill's broad class definition prevents regrettable substitutions. The cost is real but modest — reformulation of packaging, at a time when several states had already banned PFAS food packaging, so compliant alternatives already existed. On balance the trade favors the public, though the compressed timeline (effective January 1, 2025, weeks after introduction) left little runway for the smallest suppliers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from September 27, 2024 until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and was never taken up again.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the Keep Food Containers Safe from PFAS Act of 2024 on September 27, 2024, with 22 original cosponsors including Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, which is the standard first step that gives a committee control over whether it moves forward.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, at which point the bill expired.

Because the bill had an effective date of January 1, 2025, it needed to pass within weeks of introduction — an almost impossible schedule without priority treatment from House leadership and the committee, which never came.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and food-packaging producers that make or use PFAS coatings keep their market untouched by federal law; no federal costs or reformulation obligations were imposed on them because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican cosponsor out of 224 House Republicans alongside 21 Democrats, and no vote was ever taken, so party positions beyond a single Republican's support are unknown.

industries.note: The bill directly bans their product from a major use — food packaging — ending those sales nationwide. Their interest in continuing to sell PFAS-coated packaging runs against the public's interest in not ingesting persistent chemicals.

industries.industry: Food packaging and paper goods manufacturers
industries.note: Producers using PFAS coatings would face reformulation costs, while makers of PFAS-free alternatives would gain a level playing field and a larger market. Several states had already enacted similar bans, so many suppliers had compliant products available.
These businesses do not make packaging but buy it; switching to PFAS-free options could raise supply costs modestly while reducing the PFAS their packaging delivers to customers.
